title: DNS in Depth
subtitle: Watch a cold DNS lookup walk from resolver to root, TLD and authoritative server, then see how TTLs, GeoDNS and failover bend the answer.
learn: The difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative server
How root, TLD and authoritative servers cooperate to answer one question
What A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and TXT records are for
How TTL and caching trade speed against how fast changes spread
How GeoDNS and DNS-based failover steer users, and where they lag

steps.title: Names are not addresses
steps.body: Your browser wants example.com, but networks deliver data to IP addresses (numbers like 203.0.113.7). Something must translate the name into a number, and no single computer knows every name. DNS, the Domain Name System, solves this with a hierarchy of servers. Each knows only a small slice. Layers of caching mean most lookups never travel far.
steps.idea: DNS is a distributed, cached phone book arranged in layers, not one big database.
steps.caption: The browser has a name and needs an IP address.

steps.title: Ask the recursive resolver
steps.body: The operating system hands the question to a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public provider. A resolver does the whole chase for you and returns one final answer. It also keeps a cache, so if anyone nearby asked recently, it answers instantly. Here its cache has nothing for this name (a cache miss), so it must ask servers higher up. The 2 ms is just the short hop from the browser to the resolver.
steps.idea: A recursive resolver does the legwork for clients and remembers the results.
steps.caption: The browser asks the resolver, and the resolver's cache has no answer.

steps.title: Root: who runs .com?
steps.body: The animation shows the resolver asking a root server. The resolver already knows the addresses of the 13 root server names. Each name is served by many machines worldwide (anycast: machines share one address and you reach the nearest). The root does not know example.com. But it knows who runs each top-level domain such as .com, so it replies with a referral, meaning 'ask them instead'. In real life the resolver has usually cached the root and .com referrals, so most lookups skip straight to the authoritative server.
steps.idea: The root only points to the right TLD servers. It never stores individual sites.
steps.caption: The root refers the resolver to the .com servers.

steps.title: TLD: who runs example.com?
steps.body: The resolver asks again, this time a .com TLD (top-level domain) server. TLD servers know, for every registered .com name, which name servers its owner chose (stored as NS records). The reply is another referral, to example.com's own name servers. Still no IP address yet, just a closer signpost. Each step of the chase gets nearer to the owner.
steps.idea: The TLD tier maps each registered domain to its authoritative name servers.
steps.caption: The TLD server refers the resolver to example.com's servers.

steps.title: Authoritative: the real answer
steps.body: An authoritative server holds the real records for a zone, the set of records one owner manages. It answers with the A record 203.0.113.7 and a TTL (time to live) of 300 seconds, meaning 'you may reuse this answer for 5 minutes'. The resolver saves it and passes it to the browser. Count the time: about 2 ms from browser to resolver, then about 22 ms each to the root, TLD and authoritative servers. The cold lookup totals 2 + 66 = 68 ms, about 70.
steps.idea: Only the authoritative server is the source of truth. Everything else is a cached copy.
steps.caption: The authoritative server answers. The resolver caches it and replies.

steps.title: Record types
steps.body: A zone holds more than one kind of record. A maps a name to an IPv4 address and AAAA to an IPv6 address. CNAME says one name is an alias for another, so www can follow example.com. MX names the mail servers. TXT holds free text, used for domain verification and email rules such as SPF (a list of servers allowed to send your mail). Here the resolver asks for www and gets back the alias plus its target address. A CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex (the bare domain, like example.com).
steps.idea: Pick the record type by purpose: address (A, AAAA), alias (CNAME), mail (MX), metadata (TXT).
steps.caption: The resolver asks for www and follows a CNAME to an A record.

steps.title: TTL and caching
steps.body: Two seconds later, another user behind the same resolver asks for example.com. The resolver answers from its cache in about 2 ms. No root, TLD or authoritative server is contacted. Each cached answer carries a TTL that counts down, here from 300 to 298. At zero the answer is thrown away and fetched again. Browsers and operating systems cache too, so the real number of lookups is even lower.
steps.idea: A longer TTL means faster lookups and less load, but changes take longer to spread.
steps.caption: Warm cache: one hop, answer in about 2 ms.

steps.title: GeoDNS: different answers by place
steps.body: The owner runs one site in the US and one in Europe. A GeoDNS authoritative server looks at who is asking and returns the nearest origin. It usually sees only the resolver's IP address, or a client-subnet hint (a shortened copy of the user's network address that the resolver may pass along). Here a user in Europe uses a resolver in Frankfurt, so the answer is the EU address. The user's connections then take about 15 ms instead of about 90 ms. The 60 s TTL lets steering change quickly. It is only a guess: a user on a distant resolver can be sent to the wrong region.
steps.idea: GeoDNS picks the answer by the asker's location, which is only as accurate as the resolver tells it.
steps.caption: The authoritative server returns the EU address, and the browser connects there.

steps.title: DNS-based failover
steps.body: Now the EU origin dies. The authoritative server health-checks both origins, notices, and stops returning the EU address. Detection takes a few failed probes. Meanwhile resolvers and browsers still hold the old answer until its 60 s TTL runs out, and some clients ignore TTLs, so some users hit a dead server for a minute or more. That is why failover records use short TTLs. Once the cached answer expires, the next lookup returns the US address and the browser connects there.
steps.idea: DNS failover works, but it is only as fast as the TTL. Short TTLs recover faster at the cost of more lookups.
steps.caption: The EU origin is down, but cached answers still point to it.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.body: A recursive resolver chases the answer through root, TLD and authoritative servers, then caches it. Records hold different facts: addresses, aliases, mail servers, metadata. TTL is the dial between speed and agility. GeoDNS and failover both build on DNS, and both are limited by cached answers you cannot take back.
steps.idea: DNS is a cached hierarchy. Every clever trick on top inherits the TTL delay.
steps.caption: The full lookup path and the two origins it can steer to.

quiz.q: A resolver has no cached data for example.com. What is the order of servers it contacts?
options: Authoritative, then TLD, then root
Root, then TLD, then authoritative
TLD, then root, then authoritative
Root, then authoritative, skipping the TLD
quiz.why: The root points to the .com TLD servers, which point to the domain's authoritative servers, which hold the actual records.

quiz.q: You must move your site to a new IP in three days. Your A record has a 24-hour TTL. What should you do beforehand?
options: Nothing; DNS updates instantly worldwide
Raise the TTL so resolvers cache the new value longer
Lower the TTL to a few minutes well in advance, then change the IP
Switch the record to a TXT record
quiz.why: Caches keep the old answer until the TTL expires, so the TTL must be lowered at least one old-TTL period before the change.

quiz.q: You want example.com (the zone apex) to alias to a provider hostname, and also receive mail. Which is the real problem?
options: MX records cannot point to hostnames
TXT records block aliases
CNAME records only work for IPv6
A CNAME cannot coexist with other records such as MX and NS at the apex
quiz.why: A CNAME means the name is entirely an alias, so no other record types may exist at that name; apex names need NS and SOA records. Many DNS providers offer ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME flattening, which resolves the target for you and answers with plain A/AAAA records at the apex.

quiz.q: Your EU origin fails and DNS failover removes it, yet some users still see errors for a minute. Most likely cause?
options: Clients and resolvers are using cached answers until the TTL expires
The authoritative server has not noticed
GeoDNS cannot return US addresses
Root servers are overloaded
quiz.why: DNS changes only reach users as cached copies expire, so the TTL sets a floor on failover time for those clients.

quiz.q: A user in Berlin uses a public resolver that sits in the US, and GeoDNS returns the US origin. Why?
options: Root servers geolocate users
A records are always US
GeoDNS saw the resolver's location, not the user's
The TTL expired
quiz.why: The authoritative server only sees the resolver's address (unless a client-subnet hint is passed), so a distant resolver makes GeoDNS guess the wrong region.

cheatsheet.def: Server that answers clients by chasing the lookup through root, TLD and authoritative servers, and caches results.
Holds the real records for a zone. Its answers are the source of truth; all other copies are caches.
Root refers to TLD servers (.com, .org); TLD servers refer to each domain's name servers via NS records.
Map a name to an IPv4 / IPv6 address. A name can have several, which gives crude load spreading.
Makes a name an alias of another name. Cannot share a name with other records, so not allowed at the zone apex. Providers' ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME flattening can work around this.
MX lists mail servers with priorities. TXT holds text for SPF, DKIM, DMARC and domain-ownership checks.
Seconds a cached answer may be reused. Rule of thumb: about 60 s for failover records, 300-3600 s for most records, up to a day for rarely changed ones.
Authoritative server varies answers by asker location or origin health. Limited by resolver accuracy and TTL lag.
